newsitem.title: UK: Budget seen lifting BT UK earnings two pct.
newsitem.headline: Budget seen lifting BT UK earnings two pct.

text.p: The Labour budget should help lift British Telecommunications Plc's UK earnings by 1.5 to 2.0 percent, excluding changes to pension fund tax credits, and analysts said on Wednesday the telephone giant had got away lightly.

A windfall earnings tax burden of around 500 million pounds will be eased because it is due in two instalments over two years and BT also gains around 65 million pounds per year from a two percentage point reduction in the rate of corporation tax to 31 percent.
"It's about a two percent enhancement to BT's UK earnings as a result of the Chancellor's budget today," said Andrew Harrington, telecoms analyst at Salomon Brothers.

"I'm sure they feel peeved by the 500 million pound windfall tax...but the fact is I think they have got away lightly and I think that is good for shareholders. But I would be very surprised if they went to court over this."

Some analysts expect BT's shares to rise around 10p to 464.5p on Thursday, helped by relief that BT's share of a one-off windfall tax on the earnings of privatised utilities was half of some expectations.

Experts say that BT may inject 1.4 billion pounds into its pension funds to make up for a shortfall, after the government said tax credits paid to pension funds and companies would be abolished with immediate effect.
"The net effect of the budget is positive if you don't look at ACT changes which may need additional funding for pension funds," said Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming.

British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said earlier that BT would be among privatised utilities who would be taxed to raise a total of 5.2 billion pounds as part of Labour's 3.5 billion pound programme to get the young and long-term unemployed back to work.

Despite BT's threats of a possible legal challenge if it were stung hard by a windfall tax, few analysts believe the company will risk such a move although some say it could have a 50/50 chance of winning its case in European courts.
"My judgement is that they will decide that the risk-reward ratio simply does not warrant it," said Harrington.

Ehrenberg also noted it would not be in BT's interest to put a strain on its relationship with the government at a time when BT is hoping to win an early release from a ban on it using its extensive national network for broadcasting entertainment services.
"This ban is up for review in 1998 and there are signs that the government is willing to phase out this ban between 1998 and 2001," he said.
"We continue to believe that a legal challenge is not probable."
BT said it would decide how to proceed once the Finance Bill had been published.
